title: Marduk and Tiamat
paragraphs: In the beginning, the poem says, there was no sky above and no earth below, only two waters: Apsu, the sweet water beneath the ground, and Tiamat, the salt sea. Their mingling produced the first gods, who played and made noise in the shallows. Apsu, disturbed by their endless motion, decided to destroy them; Tiamat urged patience, but he would not listen.

The plan failed. Ea, god of wisdom, put Apsu to sleep with a spell and killed him, then built his house on the dead god's body. Furious, Tiamat raised an army of monsters and gave the Tablet of Destinies to her consort, Kingu.

Marduk, a young storm god, agreed to fight on one condition: if he won, the assembled gods would acknowledge him as supreme. He armed himself with bow, mace, and net, mounted the four winds, and met Tiamat in single combat. When she opened her mouth to swallow him, he drove a wind into her jaws, shot an arrow through her heart, and split her body like a shell.

From the two halves he made the vault of heaven and the floor of the earth; her eyes became the sources of the Tigris and Euphrates. He shaped humanity from Kingu's blood, to serve the gods, and the gods built Babylon for him. Enuma Elish was recited at Babylon's New Year festival. Copies from different centuries disagree, and in Assyrian versions Ashur takes Marduk's place.

title: Inanna in the Underworld
paragraphs: Inanna, queen of heaven and goddess of love and war, set her mind on the underworld, the land of no return ruled by her older sister Ereshkigal. Before leaving she told her servant Ninshubur: if I have not come back in three days, go to the gods and plead for me. Then she dressed in her finest ornaments and set out.

At each of the seven gates she gave up one ornament: crown, lapis beads, a double strand, breastplate, kohl, measuring rod and line, and robe. By the seventh gate she stood naked and bowed low. Ereshkigal's judges, the Anunnaki, fixed the eye of death on her, and she died, hung on a hook like meat.

Ninshubur went to Enlil, then to the moon god Nanna; neither would help. Enki, god of wisdom, understood what had happened. From the dirt beneath his fingernails he made two small creatures who slipped into the underworld and mourned with Ereshkigal in her pain. In gratitude she offered them a gift; they asked for Inanna's body, sprinkled it with the water of life, and Inanna rose.

But the underworld demands a substitute from anyone who leaves. Inanna returned with demons and refused to hand over her sons or her servant. At last she reached her husband Dumuzi, dressed in fine clothes and seated on her throne, and she gave him to them. He fled, and his sister Geshtinanna wept. Later Akkadian tellings end differently; the Sumerian copies disagree in places.

title: Gilgamesh and Enkidu
source_ref: Epic of Gilgamesh, Standard Babylonian version, tablets I–II
paragraphs: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, was two-thirds god and one-third human, and no wall could hold his energy. He worked his people to exhaustion on building projects and claimed brides on their wedding nights. The people of Uruk complained to the gods, and the gods answered: the goddess Aruru shaped a rival from clay, Enkidu, a hairy wild man who ran with gazelles and freed animals from hunters' traps.

A hunter brought word of him to Uruk, and Gilgamesh sent a temple woman, Shamhat, to civilise the wild man. She taught him human speech, bread, beer, and clothing; he learned shame, longing, and loneliness. When she told him about Gilgamesh, Enkidu set off for Uruk, wanting to see the king whose strength everyone praised.

They met in the street and wrestled until the doorposts shook. Gilgamesh threw Enkidu, but the fight ended in admiration, not resentment. They embraced and swore friendship, and Enkidu became the one person who could speak honestly to the king.

Restless, Gilgamesh proposed a quest to the Cedar Forest, home of the guardian Humbaba, to cut cedar and win lasting fame. Enkidu protested: he knew that forest. The elders of Uruk warned that the road was long and the enemy strong, but Gilgamesh ignored them, and the two set out. The epic was copied by scribes for well over a thousand years; its tablets come from several periods, and no single copy preserves the whole poem.

title: The Guardian of the Forest
paragraphs: The Cedar Forest lay far to the west, and the god Enlil had set the monster Humbaba there to terrify intruders. The poem describes a face like coiled entrails, a roar like a flood, breath like fire. Gilgamesh and Enkidu marched for days and nights, and each morning Gilgamesh woke from bad dreams; Enkidu reassured him, though the dreams grew darker.

At the forest edge they hesitated. Shamash, the sun god, sent winds that pinned Humbaba's arms, and the two heroes closed in. Humbaba begged for his life and offered to serve them, even to guard the forest for them. Enkidu urged Gilgamesh to finish it before the god could change his mind; Gilgamesh struck with his sword, and they cut a great cedar for a door.

The consequences fell on Enkidu. Enlil was furious, and the gods decreed that one of the two must die. Enkidu dreamed of the underworld and of the gods in council. He cursed the door they had made, then fell ill. For twelve days he grew worse while Gilgamesh watched for a sign and refused to believe what was coming.

When Enkidu died, Gilgamesh covered the body and mourned for seven days and seven nights. Then he left Uruk and wandered, terrified by the thought that he too must die. The killing is told differently in older Sumerian poems and in the Standard Babylonian epic, and surviving copies preserve different lines, so details vary.

title: The Flood
source_ref: Epic of Gilgamesh, tablet XI; Atrahasis
paragraphs: Beyond the waters at the edge of the world lived Utnapishtim, the one man the gods had given everlasting life. He told Gilgamesh a secret: the great gods had decided to send a flood. Ea, god of wisdom, was bound by an oath not to warn humanity, so he spoke to the reed wall of Utnapishtim's house instead, and the man inside understood.

Ea told him to tear down his house and build a boat, equal in length and width and roofed like the deep. He was to bring his family, his craftsmen, and every kind of living thing. Utnapishtim feasted his workers and sealed the door when the rain began. The storm came at dawn, and the waters rose over the land.

Even the gods were frightened. They fled to the highest heaven and crouched like dogs, and Ishtar wept, crying that she had agreed to a war that destroyed her own people. For six days and seven nights the wind blew; on the seventh the waters quieted, and the boat came to rest on Mount Nimush.

Utnapishtim sent out a dove, which found nothing and returned; then a swallow; then a raven, which found the water receding and did not return. He poured a libation and burned incense, and the gods gathered over the offering like flies. Enlil was angry that a human had escaped, but Ea argued that the punishment had been too harsh, and Enlil blessed Utnapishtim and his wife with immortality. The flood appears in several Mesopotamian versions, including Atrahasis, with different heroes and reasons for the gods' anger.

title: The Plant of Immortality
paragraphs: After Enkidu's death, Gilgamesh wandered in search of Utnapishtim, the only human who had escaped death. He crossed the mountains of Mashu and the tunnel of the sun, passed the scorpion-men, and came to a garden where trees bore jewels. By the sea the brewer Siduri advised him to eat, drink, and enjoy his children while he could. He refused: he was afraid to die.

With the boatman Urshanabi he crossed the waters of death, poling so the boat would not touch the water, and came to Utnapishtim. He heard the flood story, then asked how this man had won life without end. Utnapishtim set him a test, to stay awake for six days and seven nights. Gilgamesh fell asleep at once, and the loaves baked each day beside him proved how long he had slept.

At his wife's urging, Utnapishtim told Gilgamesh about a thorny plant that grew at the bottom of the sea and made an old man young again. Gilgamesh tied stones to his feet, dived, and pulled it up, though the thorns tore his hands. He set off home with the plant, and on the way he stopped at a pool to bathe.

A snake smelled the plant, took it, and slipped away, shedding its skin as it went. Gilgamesh sat down and wept; he had travelled so far and lost everything to a snake. He came back to Uruk with empty hands. Yet the poem ends with him beside Urshanabi before the city walls, naming the brickwork and gardens, the one thing he built that would last. The epic was edited over many centuries, and copies differ.
